# MAM Is a Dataset

Script for a narrated slideshow video.

| Image | Narration |
|-------|-----------|
| ![title card](img/thumb-title-card.png) | This video is a follow-up to my video, "What is MAM?" I hope it will be one of many such follow-ups. One of the trickiest and most important things to understand about MAM is that it is not an edition of the Hebrew Bible. It is a dataset that can be used to create editions of the Hebrew Bible. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 sources](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-sources.png) | For example, here's Psalm 5 verse 9 in five different editions created from the MAM dataset. Some of them format ketiv/qere differently. Some of them include MAM's documentation notes. Some do not. Those that do include the notes display them in different ways. |
| ![Psalm 15:1 qamats](img/thumb-psalm-15v1-qamats.png) | MAM sometimes even presents editions with two or more versions of the same word. For example, there is a _qamats_ in this Psalm 15:1 word that can be either _qatan_ or _gadol_, according to different sets of rules. MAM presents both, as you can see from the JSON encoding here. (I've shown the JSON with _qamats qatan_ upside down to make the distinction clearer). Most editions choose one or the other, but some really weird editions may want to show both, like my "Phonetic Tanakh" does, as shown here! |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 0](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-0.png) | Here's Psalm 5:9 again, with the contents of MAM shown as JSON on one side, and the way one particular edition chooses to render that contents also shown. There's a lot of details there, but the main point is that MAM is written in a kind of computer language called a markup language, and each edition is free to interpret that markup as it likes. Another way of putting it is that MAM is written in a language similar to HTML, and different editions can interpret MAM differently, similar to the way different CSS code can style HTML differently. It is important to note that the analogy to styling includes the usual somewhat superficial questions like color but also more substantive questions like whether an element is even shown or not! |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 1](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-1.png) | Let's walk through this verse element by element. The first item highlighted is the simplest kind of thing in MAM's markup: a plain string of pointed Hebrew text. Here it's the divine name יְהֹוָ֤ה — with its vowels and its cantillation accent. You can see that same string highlighted in the rendered edition on the left. The majority of MAM's content is plain strings just like this one. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 2](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-2.png) | Not everything is a plain string, though. This highlighted item is a template object: `{"tmpl_name": "מ:לגרמיה-2"}`. It encodes the legarmeih — the bold vertical bar that appears close to the preceding word in the rendered edition, as highlighted on the left. Legarmeih and paseq share the same Unicode character, but they have different functions in the text. By encoding it as a named template, MAM lets each edition render — or suppress — the legarmeih as it sees fit. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 3](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-3.png) | Next is `{"tmpl_name": "ר0"}`. The letter ר (Resh) is MAM's shorthand for a family of poetry-layout templates. ר0 specifically is an extra division point used when a verse has an odd number of stiches, so that the verse can be displayed in balanced two-column poetry layout. In this Wikisource edition, it appears as a non-breaking space — just enough to push the following text into the right column. An edition that doesn't use multi-column poetry layout can treat ר0 as nothing at all. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 4](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-4.png) | Back to a plain string: `"נְחֵ֬נִי בְצִדְקָתֶ֗ךָ"` — "lead me in your righteousness." Highlighted on the left. Together with the divine name from step one, this is the plain pointed Hebrew text of the first stich of the verse. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 5](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-5.png) | The first `{"tmpl_name": "ר1"}` template. ר1 tells an edition to begin the next stich on its own line, indented one level. On the left, you can see both the line-break marker and the indentation at the start of the second line highlighted. An edition that renders prose rather than poetry can treat ר1 as a simple word space and ignore the indentation entirely. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 6](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-6.png) | Two more plain strings: the word `"לְמַ֥עַן"` — "for the sake of" — and a following space `" "`. Highlighted on the left. Note that the space is its own separate item in the JSON array rather than being embedded in the next word. This is a common pattern in MAM that gives editions flexibility in how adjacent elements are joined together. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 7](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-7.png) | Here we have a `{"tmpl_name": "נוסח"}` — a nusach, or textual-variant, template. Parameter 1 is the main reading of the word, `"שׁוֹרְﬞרָ֑י"`, which includes a rafeh mark above one of the letters. Parameter 2 documents an alternate reading using a hataf vowel instead: `"שׁוֹרֲרָ֑י (חטף)"`. This Wikisource edition displays only the main form, which you can see highlighted on the left. But the alternate reading is encoded in the MAM data, available to any edition that wants to display it. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 8](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-8.png) | The second `{"tmpl_name": "ר1"}` — another poetry line break with one indent, starting the third and final stich of the verse. On the left, the line-break marker and indentation for the third line are highlighted, mirroring what we saw for the second line. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 9](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-9.png) | This is `{"tmpl_name": "כו\"ק"}` — the standard ketiv/qere template. Ketiv means "what is written" and qere means "what is read aloud." Parameter 1 is the ketiv, the unpointed form as it appears in the manuscript. Parameter 2 is the pointed qere, the form traditionally pronounced. In the rendered edition on the left, both appear together — the ketiv in gray, the qere in the normal reading color. Different editions can choose to show only one, or neither, or both in some other arrangement. |
| ![Psalm 5:9 mpplus step 10](img/thumb-psalm-5v9-mpplus-step-10.png) | The final element: a space and the closing words `"לְפָנַ֣י דַּרְכֶּֽךָ׃"` — "before me, your way." The verse-end mark, the sof pasuq (׃), is part of this plain string — no separate template is needed for it. Highlighted on the left, this is the end of the verse. And with that, we've walked through every element of the MAM encoding of Psalm 5:9 — a mix of plain strings carrying the Hebrew text, and named templates carrying structural and editorial information that each edition can interpret in its own way. |
